newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Police examine death of Australian denied euthanasia.
newsitem.headline: Police examine death of Australian denied euthanasia.

text.p: Australian police said on Tuesday they were investigating the death of a terminally-ill woman who was denied access to Australia's short-lived voluntary euthanasia law.
Police in the outback Northern Territory said they were preparing a report into the death of 56-year-old former nursing sister Esther Wild, who died after a drug-induced coma.
"We are preparing a report for the coroner," a police spokeswoman told Reuters by telephone from Darwin, capital of the Northern Territory.
As part of the investigation police will question Dr Philip Nitschke, who helped four people die under Australia's voluntary euthanasia law -- the world's first assisted suicide law.
Nitschke said he had been asked by police to make himself available for interview and to provide copies of medical records relating to Wild's death.

Wild, who was suffering cancer, died last month after spending four days in a coma brought on by pain-relieving drugs. Her death was announced by Nitschke, who described it at the time as a form of "slow euthanasia".

"I'm not too sure that what we did was particularly ethical and I'm not too sure what we did was particularly moral," Nitschke told Australian Broadcasting Corporation radio on Tuesday. "I think it was perfectly legal, and therein is the problem we've got," he said.
Wild had been one of two people who had completed the formal requirements of the Rights of the Terminally Act when the Australian parliament quashed the territory's law on March 26.

The national parliament has constitutional power over Australia's three territories but the country's six states enjoy The Northern Territory's euthanasia law came into effect in July 1996, after which Nitschke helped four people commit suicide with a computer-administered lethal injection.
Despite federal parliament's vote to overturn the law, which was taken on conscience rather than party lines, polls show about 75 percent of Australians support euthanasia.
Nitschke said after Wild's death that she had been rendered comatose to relieve the "relentless physical and emotional pain" of her illness.
"We go down these paths because we've got nowhere else to go," Nitschke said. "I don't think it's particularly ethical to deny a dying person's last wish and that is that they die quickly."
